identity.title: Glycogen synthase AfGsy2 regulates mycelial growth, stress response, predatory activity, and chlamydospore development in the nematode-trapping fungus Arthrobotrys flagrans.

content.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Glycogen is a universal carbon and energy reserve that plays crucial roles in fungal stress adaptation, cellular homeostasis, and predatory activity. However, the role of glycogen metabolism in nematode-trapping fungi has largely remained unexplored. Here, we performed a systematic functional characterization of AfGsy2, the glycogen synthase-encoding gene in the biocontrol fungus Arthrobotrys flagrans. METHODS: Using a CRISPR-Cas9-mediated deletion mutant, together with overexpression and complementation strains, we investigated the involvement of AfGsy2 in mycelial growth, stress tolerance, trap formation, nematicidal activity against Caenorhabditis elegans, chlamydospore production and germination, and glycogen accumulation. Subcellular localization was examined using an AfGsy2-GFP fusion protein. RESULTS: Deletion of AfGsy2 reduced hyphal growth on both nutrient-rich and nutrient-poor media but enhanced tolerance to osmotic, salt, and oxidative stresses, suggesting that blocked glycogen synthesis may trigger metabolic rerouting toward alternative stress-protective compounds. Notably, the DeltaAfGsy2 mutants exhibited reduced trap production and nematicidal activity against C. elegans, whereas overexpression of AfGsy2 accelerated these processes, suggesting a link between glycogen metabolism and predatory activity. Moreover, AfGsy2 positively regulated chlamydospore production, glycogen accumulation, and chlamydospore germination. AfGsy2-GFP predominantly localized to the vacuoles of chlamydospores, and complementation restored the mutant phenotypes to wild-type levels. DISCUSSION: Collectively, these findings uncover a link between glycogen metabolism and growth, stress resilience, sporulation, and predatory activity in A. flagrans, and establish a molecular foundation for the rational improvement of nematode-trapping fungi. Together, these results identify AfGsy2 as a pleiotropic regulator linking glycogen metabolism to biocontrol-related traits.
